observation.visible_scene: Open ocean under a flat overcast sky, filmed from a boat. A large dark grey whale lies at the surface with its body horizontal, head to the left (a pale jaw/mouth patch visible) and tail to the right. One dark, white-mottled fin/flipper is raised vertically out of the water near the middle of the back. In the early frames two seabirds are silhouetted in the sky on the right; from mid-clip a white boat railing and a rounded white object intrude at the bottom edge.
visible_changes: The whale's body stays essentially in place at the surface throughout, only bobbing slightly with the swell; no horizontal travel or dive occurs within the excerpt.
The raised fin tilts/rotates gradually, its tip shifting from a near-vertical lean to a more upright/right-leaning angle, while remaining out of the water.

The horizon line rises and falls across the frame (e.g. high in early frames, lower in mid frames, then high again near the end), indicating camera/boat tilt and rocking rather than the whale moving vertically.
The white boat railing and rounded object appear at the bottom edge in the middle portion of the clip and are absent at the start and end, reflecting camera framing changes.
The two birds drift out of the upper-right sky over the first few frames; the sky is otherwise empty.
White mottling/scarring on the whale's back and the raised fin persists unchanged.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the whale subsequently submerges, sounds, or begins swimming is not shown; the segment is a near-static floating pose.
The exact identity of the raised appendage (pectoral fin vs. dorsal fin) and the species are not determinable from these frames alone.
What caused the boat to enter/leave the bottom of frame (camera zoom vs. operator movement) is unseen.
uncertain_details: Small apparent shifts in the whale's position relative to the frame are hard to separate from camera shake/boat motion, so the whale's own movement is minimal and uncertain in magnitude.
The slight change in fin angle could be passive bobbing rather than active movement.
Reflections on the wet body are not distinguished from separate white patches.
